Dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is the difference between the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) caused by the presence of the reason (*hetu*);
that which possesses this is a probative statement characterized by dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat*).

The exposition of the application of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) by way of similarity, and the demonstration that everything conditioned is momentary: therein, in order to show the application of the essential reason by way of similarity, the Blessed One, relying on the Sautrāntika view, stated:
"Everything conditioned is momentary."
That is now explained:
the collection of things produced by causes and conditions having come together and combined is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
it is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), because it exists only at the very moment of its arising.
An Examination of the Destruction of All Conditioned Things:
"First of all, every object such as a jar is seen to undergo destruction when in proximity to a hammer or other such causes.

In that regard, if the very nature by which the jar or other object perishes in its final state already exists in it at the moment of its arising, then it would have to perish immediately after its production."
It is evident that this [entity] is momentary.
Or rather, its very nature is such that it was produced by its own cause so as to perish after having remained for a certain period of time.

In that case, even when a hammer or similar object is present, this very same nature would belong to it, and thus it would have to remain for that same duration once again; and since it would be the same yet again, it would never perish at all.

Therefore, if it were to arise with a duration of two moments, then because it would possess that same two-moment duration in the second moment just as in the first, it would continue to persist for another two moments.
Thus, even in the third moment, because it possesses that same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it does not perish at all.
One might argue: "That entity was produced by its own cause as something stable; it is destroyed by a forceful, opposing agent such as a hammer."
That is incorrect; how, moreover, is this tenable— that it does not perish because of its stability,
yet its destruction is brought about by a contrary force?
For it is not possible that Devadatta both lives and yet undergoes death;
if, on the other hand, he perishes,
how then could that entity have been produced by its own causes as something imperishable?
For it is not tenable to say that something both dies and possesses the nature of being immortal;
therefore, since destruction is impossible at any time for that which is imperishable,
and because destruction is observed [in experience], [it follows that things are perishable].
We accept that this entity is indeed perishable, having arisen from its own causes;
therefore, it perishes as soon as it has arisen. In this way, momentary destruction is established.
The formal argument (prayoga) should be stated as follows: Whatever has a perishable nature does not endure beyond that [moment], just like the nature of a jar existing in its final moment.
And since form and so forth possess a perishable nature at the time of their arising, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
This is the formulation of a reason based on essential nature without qualifications (*nirviśeṣaṇasvabhāvahetu*).
If entities perish moment by moment, how then can there be recognition such as "this is that very same thing"? It is said:

because of the continuous arising of successive moments that are similar [to the preceding], and due to the persistence of ignorance (*avidyā*), at the very time of the destruction of the prior moment, another moment similar to it arises.

Because there is an absence of difference in that aspect and because there is no interruption by non-existence, the cognition of a determination of non-difference—“this is that very same thing”—arises for ordinary people even though there is a distinction.

Furthermore, such a cognition as “this is that very same thing” is indeed observed even in the case of things that are absolutely distinct, such as grass or hair that has been cut and grown back again.
Why, then, should it not be possible here as well?
Therefore, it is established that all conditioned phenomena are momentary; this is the application of an essential nature as a reason (svabhāvahetu) without any qualification.
Likewise, there is another formulation without qualification: whatever exists is all impermanent, just like a pot;
and these [entities] under discussion exist, as they are cognized by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Likewise, there is another intrinsic reason (*svabhāvahetu*) for proving that the Veda has a personal author:
whatever is a sentence is of human origin,
just like the sentence of a man on the street.
And this statement—
“One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra”—
is an application of a reason whose nature consists of a qualification.
An example of the use with a qualification is as follows: whatever possesses origination is all impermanent, such as a pot;
and sound possesses origination.
An entity that has turned away from what has not yet arisen is called "arisen.

When that very exclusion is stated as distinct by means of the exclusion of other exclusions— namely, as "the arising of the entity"— then the nature itself, as qualified by a property that is its own essence through an imagined distinction,
is the logical reason (*hetu*).

The formulation of a reason whose nature consists of a distinct qualification is as follows—the formulation of one with a distinct qualification: "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a pot; and sound is produced."
One might object: "The term *citragu* (‘one who has brindled cows’) is an instance of a word with a distinct qualifier (*bhinnaviśeṣaṇa*).

Just as in this compound *citrago*, there exists a word expressing a distinct qualifier, such is not the case with the word *kṛtaka* (‘produced’), for it contains no element whatsoever that expresses a distinct qualifier.
Therefore, how can it serve as an example of a word with a distinct qualifier? If this is asked:
It is said: A thing whose own nature (*svabhāva*) is produced while depending upon the operation of another is called "produced" (*kṛtaka*).

In this context, the word "produced," by its very nature, expresses a nature that depends upon the operation of another, and thus denotes precisely that which possesses a distinct qualification (*bhinnaviśeṣaṇa*).

The formulation of a reason whose nature consists of a distinct qualification that has been employed is the formulation of a nature with an employed distinct qualification: "That which varies according to the variation of conditions is produced, such as smoke."
And sound is differentiated by the differentiation of its conditions (*pratyaya*).
"Condition" (*pratyaya*) means cause; that which has the nature of being differentiated by the differentiation of that [cause] is "differentiated by the differentiation of conditions."

The meaning is that its greatness [is due to] the greatness of its cause, and its smallness [is due to] the smallness of its cause; for here the term *pratyayabhedabhedi*—which expresses distinct qualifiers—is employed, and thus it is one whose distinct qualifiers have been employed.

Furthermore, the demonstration of the various subdivisions of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is for the purpose of removing confusion, in order to establish that even when there is a conceptualization of a difference in properties (*dharmabheda*), it is indeed the essential reason alone that is employed.

The formulation of the application of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): An example of the application of the essential reason by way of dissimilarity is as follows: whatever is not non-abiding immediately thereafter does not have a perishable nature at that time, such as space.

Furthermore, since form and the other aggregates are perishable at the time of their arising, it should be understood that in a formulation based on difference (*vyatireka*), the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is pervaded by the absence of the probans (*sādhana*); thus, the absence of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans.
Likewise, there is another formulation characterized by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): where momentariness does not exist, existence (*sattva*) also does not exist.
Just as in the case of a sky-lotus,
sound is existent;
likewise, wherever impermanence has ceased, there too the quality of having an origin has ceased.
Just as in the case of a tortoise's hair;
and sound possesses origination.
Wherever impermanence has ceased, there "producedness" (kṛtakatva) has also ceased.
Just as in the case of a hare's horn;
and sound is produced;
where there is no state of being produced, there also is no variation according to the variation of conditions.
Just as in the sky,
sound is differentiated by the differentiation of its conditions.

The examination of the application of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) through both the method of agreement (*sādharmya*) and the method of difference (*vaidharmya*). An example of the application of the effect-reason by way of agreement is as follows: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen."
And here, smoke is also an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*); it should be employed when the causal relation has been established through perception and non-perception, with the cause being the probandum.
An application by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyaprayoga*) is as follows: "Where there is no fire, smoke does not exist at all, as for example, in a great lake."

And here [the statement] "there is smoke. The formulation of non-apprehension by way of similarity (*anupalabdheḥ sādharmyavat prayogaḥ*) for the purpose of refuting the whole (*avayavin*) is as follows: whatever, being present and meeting the conditions for apprehension, is not apprehended there, that is fit for the conventional usage of being non-existent there.

Just as a horn is not found on a human head, so too the "whole" (avayavin) postulated by the opponent— which meets the conditions for perception— is not perceived here in the shards denoted by the word "jar. This is the formulation of the argument based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya).

An application based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) regarding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is as follows: whatever exists and meets the conditions for apprehension is necessarily apprehended, just like a particular such as blue;
yet here, there is no apprehension of a jar that exists and meets the conditions for apprehension.

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) must be understood as follows: in every syllogism based on similarity (*sādharmya*), the probans is pervaded by the probandum; whereas in a syllogism based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the absence of the probandum is pervaded by the absence of the probans.

The statement that the probans (sādhana) is necessarily concomitant with the probandum (sādhya), and the statement that the absence of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans, is called pervasion (vyāpti).
Therefore, once pervasion has been established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), one should not entertain the doubt anywhere that something might be a probans while [the probandum] is absent.
And thus, the probandum would not exist in that subject (*dharmin*).
This is the refutation of the inference put forward by others to prove the existence of God (*īśvara*),
wherein the pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself— encompassing all instances— is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, the spread of doubt is unavoidable, as in the inference of "being an effect" used to prove the existence of God (Īśvara).
For such is their presentation of the proof: [text continues].
In this regard, whether or not there exists another omniscient Blessed One, it is nonetheless possible to establish that Īśvara is omniscient.
For instance, in the world, there are indeed three kinds of entities: some have a definitely identified agent; [others have an unidentified agent; and others have no agent at all].
For example, things such as jars;
and some whose cessation of a definite agent is established,
such as space and so forth.
Others, moreover, have an uncertain author,
such as the earth and so forth;
yet there is no other category besides these.

In this regard, those things such as trees whose production is currently perceived, and those such as the earth whose production occurred long ago— all of these, while existing with their agency in doubt, possess an intelligent creator, just like a jar.
This reason is not unestablished (asiddha).
Because the property of being an effect (kāryatva) is established by valid cognition for all [things],
it is not contradictory either, since it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa).
Nor is there an inconclusive [reason], because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*).
To explain: first, it is observed by mental perception—assisted by repeated observation—that an effect arises from an intelligent potter.
If this [universe] were to exist even without an intelligent being, then it would never arise from an intelligent cause;

for it is impossible for an effect to be produced even once in the absence of its cause. Therefore, one should not entertain the doubt anywhere that something might be an effect and yet not have an intelligent cause.

To this, it is replied: It is indeed agreed by all disputants that a probans (*sādhana*) must lead to the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) only when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans has been established through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of a universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāre�*);

in that case, if the pervasion were grasped as being with an intelligent agent characterized by a visible body, then this reason would be an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) one—specifically a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*)—because the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is observed in things such as grass which arise even in the absence of such a probandum, just like the state of being knowable (*prameyatva*).

Nor should it be said that grass and the like are included within the subject (*pakṣa*); for that which is the very object of deviation cannot be the subject, according to the principle: "Because the reason is stated regarding what is doubtful; what is excluded [from the subject] is not a locus for the reason."

Now, one might argue that since smoke is observed even on a mountain that is impossible to climb and without the presence of fire, it is equally easy to claim that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of smoke as well. That is not so;
because the fire cannot be seen on the mountain due to its being inaccessible, it is correct that in that case the object of cognition is doubtful.

In the present case, however, it is logical that when a pervasion is apprehended with an intelligent agent qualified by a visible body, there occurs a sublation of the intelligent agent by means of the non-perception of a visible [object].

But if the pervasion is understood either with an intelligent agent possessing a visible body or with an intelligent agent in general, then— since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the probandum (either an invisible intelligent agent or an intelligent agent in general) cannot be established through the non-perception of a visible object— this reason has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika*).

Because the absence of the probans (sādhana) as necessitated by the absence of the probandum (sādhya) is unestablished [in cases such as grass and so forth], there is no pervasion (vyāpti). Thus it has been stated by the venerable Jñānaśrīmitra: "If an imperceptible agent is postulated to prevent the occurrence of the effect-ness (kāryatva) in the counter-example (vipakṣa), how can pervasion be established when the proof of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is lacking?"
If, on the other hand, with the intention of establishing a negative concomitance (vyatireka), one resorts to a visible agent,
then even the connection of that [agent] with grass and so forth clearly constitutes the observation of a counter-example (vipakṣa).
The refutation of Trilocana’s assertion of an intrinsic relationship between fire and smoke,
as stated by Trilocana:
"Just as there is an intrinsic relationship between smoke and the like with fire and the like..."
"Because the property of being an effect [is invariably concomitant] with an intelligent agent, since no qualifying condition (upādhi) for it is perceived,
and because no deviation is observed anywhere."
That is not correct; for by the word "limiting condition" (*upādhi*), some distinct entity (*arthāntara*) that must be depended upon is denoted,
and such a distinct entity need not necessarily be perceptible.
Even that which is invisible—being remote in terms of space, time, or intrinsic nature—is still possible.
Therefore, there may exist an *upādhi* (limiting condition) in the relationship between smoke and fire;
yet it is not perceived. How, then, can one say "it does not exist at all" based on mere non-perception?
As for the argument that was stated— that there is no observation of deviation— that too is "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).
For even if deviation is not observed due to the deficiency of other causal conditions, it is impossible to exclude it in all cases.
Nor does this entail a transgression of the worldly course of authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*),
for it is precisely by those authorities that doubt is prescribed when there is an absence of both proving and refuting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And yet, it does not follow from this that activity would occur everywhere on the basis of such doubt.
Because activity is possible both through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and through doubt regarding an object;
and as for what was said—
that although there is no difference in their being "other," only certain things would be functional for the Buddhists— [that is not so].
Only a certain cause [is effective], not every one;
likewise, for me as well, although there is no difference in otherness, only a certain [cause] is [effective].
"It is not the case that every entity, such as smoke and so forth, is connected by way of an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*).
This is not tenable.
Just as the fact that the entity called "smoke" is dependent upon fire is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is an intrinsic relation likewise established by valid cognition?
On what basis is this said?
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "intrinsic relation" (*svābhāvika-sambandha*)? Does it mean that it exists by itself (*svataḥ*)?
There are three alternatives: that it arises from its own cause, or that it is without a cause.
Among these, the first position is not tenable, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
Nor is the second [alternative] possible,
because it would entail the acceptance of the relation of origination from that [cause].
Or, if it were causeless, [it would follow that it arises at all times].
In that case, because there would be no restriction regarding place, time, or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the doctrine of an inherent relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*) is utterly untenable.
Furthermore, since there is merely an example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—whether by similarity or dissimilarity—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established;
for it would follow that such a relation could exist even between a camel and a blade of *gadarbha* grass, which might happen to meet by chance.
Therefore, what is called an "illustration" (nidarśana)— that is, an example—

is employed with respect to the logical reason (hetu) solely by way of recollecting the means of valid cognition that establishes the invariable concomitance (pratibandha) once it has been grasped but forgotten; it is not effective by its mere presence.
For instance: first of all, the absence of the probans is not perceived in space due to the absence of the probandum there.
For in space, just as there is the exclusion of an intelligent cause, so too there is no exclusion of a non-intelligent cause either.
Therefore, on account of what could the absence of being an effect be perceived as being conditioned by the absence [of that cause]?
[The opponent might argue: "By this, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—whereby the absence of the probans is necessitated by the absence of the probandum—is established.

[We reply: Nor is it appropriate to claim that because the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of being an effect with an intelligent agent is observed in a jar, the absence of being an effect in space (*ākāśa*) must simply follow from the absence of an intelligent agent there;

for it has already been stated that neither identity (*tādātmya*), nor causality (*tadutpatti*), nor any other natural relationship (*svābhāvikādi-sambandha*) between these two has been established by a prior means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established by mere non-perception;

furthermore, negative concomitance is not established by mere non-perception alone. For instance, by the statement "the reason is not perceived in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)," what is meant is the cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that would perceive it.
Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the effect (*kārya*) of the object of cognition (*prameya*),
according to the principle that "that which is not a cause cannot be an object. And it is not logical for the cessation of the cause to follow from the cessation of the effect.
For fire is perceived even when devoid of smoke.
However, if the existence of the object of cognition were pervaded by the existence of the means of valid cognition,
then this would indeed be logical.
This pervasion alone is impossible,
because it would entail that everyone is all-seeing;
therefore, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established by mere non-perception.

As it has been said: "The non-perception of all [other things] is doubtful, while one's own non-perception is inconclusive; for even a seed situated within the earth or water is seen not to exist [therein]."
Regarding the refutation of Vācaspati’s view:

as for what Vācaspati said—"Doubt arises only in dependence upon the recollection of specific qualities; therefore, it is proper to suspect only that which has been previously observed"—[this is incorrect].
To this it is replied: this principle is not universal. Furthermore, we speak even while conceding it for the sake of argument.

For instance, according to his own view as well, *prameyatva*, *dhūmatva*, *kāryatva*, and so forth, possess a commonality (*sajātīyatva*) by virtue of the general property of being devoid of the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*). This applies to both *kāryatva* and *dhūmatva*.

In that case, the very observation of the non-deviation of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) from the subject gives rise to suspicion regarding other [cases] as well; thus, this suspicion is raised precisely according to what is observed.
Consequently, the fault of the reason known as "doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instance" (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*) is indeed unavoidable.
And this is certainly a valid refutation.

Therefore, as for what was stated by him—"This is not a fault of the reason; therefore, it need not be refuted; and its presentation is called the point of defeat known as 'the non-exposure of a fault'"—[that is rejected].

Therefore, since this proponent has now contradicted himself by means of the point of defeat characterized as "charging with what is not to be charged," he—this "beloved of the gods"—is to be disregarded.
Regarding the impossibility [of the argument] in the inference proving a Lord (*īśvara*):

if it is argued that—just as there is pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the universals of visible fire and smoke based on perception and non-perception of those very universals whose natures are visible—there would then be no inference of another mental continuum, because at the time of grasping the pervasion, the other's mind is not included since its nature is invisible; [we reply: no.
For in that case, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is what grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*);
this is because even another's mind is visible in relation to mere self-awareness.

Furthermore, it is not tenable that the scope [of such cognition] should be merely the conventional sensory perception, merely the intellect, merely the belly, merely the painting, or merely the fire, as these are common [to many different things].
By means of this, even that [fire] would possess visibility.
Therefore, the logical principle is that the pervasion of smoke by fire is established through perception and non-perception precisely by means of the visible fire.

Furthermore, if by this [inference] the state of being preceded by a mere intelligent being is what is being proved, then the proof is subject to the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
However, if what is being proved is the state of being preceded by an intelligent being qualified by such attributes as being one, eternal, and omniscient, [then the fault does not apply].

In that case, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the probans (*sādhana*), namely "being an effect," with the probandum (*sādhya*) as qualified by such attributes has not been established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), there is the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*).
If it is argued that the pervasion is taken in a general sense and the establishment of the specific [attribute] occurs through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatābalāt*),
that is not tenable.

When a reason cannot function upon the subject (dharmin) without a particular qualification residing in the probandum (sādhya), the establishment of that qualification is logically justified by the force of its being a property of the subject (pakṣadharma).
For example, from smoke, the property of fire residing in a specific location such as a mountain is established.
But this does not apply to specific qualities such as being produced from grass (*tārṇatva*),
because smoke is observed on a mountain even in the absence of its being produced from grass.
Similarly, if the existence of an intelligent agent (*buddhimat*) within a body or the like is established, let it be so.
Furthermore, omniscience is not absolutely distinct [from non-omniscience],
because the state of being an effect is possible even in the case of one who is not omniscient.
Nor is omniscience established merely from the fact of being cognizant of the material cause and so forth.
This would be established if unity were established;
however, unity is not established,
because the state of being an effect is possible even when preceded by multiple agents.
Just as the head of Śakra was produced by many insects,
if it is then argued that even the head of Śakra must have been preceded by Īśvara,
then how can it serve as an example for establishing that a jar also has Īśvara as its precursor?
Now, how can the agency of the potter, which is observed, be set aside?
And how can the causality of insects and the like, which is also observed, be prevented?
Furthermore, there is no possibility of disagreement regarding the fact that many things can be causes.
"Because it has been seen.

Therefore, it is established that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans, which encompasses all instances, must necessarily be demonstrated by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the subject of the example (*dṛṣ�ṭāntadharmī*).
Furthermore, if an intelligent agent is to be proven as being eternal, unitary, and omniscient, this [reason] is also contradictory (*viruddha*).
Because "being an effect" (kāryatva) is pervaded by [the qualities of] being impermanent, manifold, and non-omniscient, as well as by intelligence;
for it is said here that a reason is "contradictory" (viruddha) when it proves the opposite of what is to be proven (sādhya).

And since this [reason] proves the opposite of the sādhya, let us for now set aside the composition of this treatise on exposing the refutation of Īśvara, which has arisen in the course of our discussion.

Regarding the formulations based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), there may be a doubt as to whether the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) are established; this is now refuted. Indeed, in a proof-statement based on similarity, only the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated, not the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); and in one based on dissimilarity, only the negative concomitance is stated.
But it is not positive concomitance (anvaya).
If it is asked, "How then is the three-featured logical mark (trirūpa-liṅga) described by these two?"—
this is not a fault.
Because when a proof-statement (sādhana-vākya) possessing positive concomitance (sādharmya) is presented, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is understood by implication alone;

and if the negative concomitance were not grasped, one would have to entertain the possibility of a reversal (viparyaya), namely that even in the absence of the probandum (sādhya), there is no absence of the probans (sādhana).
In this way, there would be an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) itself;

for even when the probans (*sādhana*) exists, the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent—this is the implied meaning. Likewise, when a statement of proof characterized by negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*) is presented, positive concomitance is understood through the very force of that implication.

For if both the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) were grasped through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), a reversal would have to be possible— namely, that something could be a probans without being a probandum—
and thus there would be no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) at all,
because the probans would exist even in the absence of the probandum; this is the implicit force [of the argument].
Therefore, both types of formal argument (prayoga) reveal the three-featured logical mark (trirūpaliṅga); thus, there is no fault.
The determination of the means of valid cognition that apprehends pervasion:
now, [we shall explain] in which substratum (dharmin) the pervasion between the probandum and the probans is to be apprehended,
and by what means of valid cognition.

Both of these are explained for the sake of easy understanding: some maintain that the pervasion of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), characterized by existence, must be apprehended in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) itself;
their position is the doctrine of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*).

Others hold that the pervasion must be apprehended in an example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), such as a jar, by means of both the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*).
For them, external pervasion (bahirvyāpti) is intended.
For other types of essential reasons (svabhāvahetu), effect reasons (kāryahetu), and non-perception reasons (anupalambhahetu), the pervasion must be grasped only within the example.
In that regard, concerning the application of the term "tree" to the state of being a *śiṃśipā* tree:

In the case of the probandum and the example, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is to be grasped through perception and non-apprehension. However, in the case of existence (*sattva*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), it is established by the two means of valid cognition consisting of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*), or else by the means of valid cognition that sublates the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyayabādhakapramāṇa*), characterized by the exclusion of succession and simultaneity. This is because [momentariness] is established either through the capacity of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) or through conceptual determination (*vikalpasiddhi*), while [existence] is being doubted as being either a real entity (*vastutva*) or a non-entity (*avastutva*).
In the case of the subject (*dharmin*) that constitutes the counter-example (*vipakṣa*),

the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), such as smoke, with its cause, such as fire, must be apprehended— either through threefold perception and non-perception, or through fivefold perception and non-perception— in an example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) such as a kitchen.
However, the pervasion of non-apprehension with the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent" is established by perception itself;

whereas for other [reasons], such as certain essential natures (*svabhāva-hetu*) or effects (*kārya-hetu*), they must be grasped after having been inferred through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to their respective natures.
An examination of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not ascertained, the reason possesses the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This is of three kinds: the uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) and the common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
And [the reason] whose exclusion from the opposite is doubtful.
Among these, an uncommon inconclusive [reason] is, for example: "The living body possesses a self, because it possesses breath and so forth, like another living body, and like a jar."
It is not certain that this reason is pervaded by the self in other living bodies;
nor is it certain that it is absent from the pot, which is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), due to the absence of the self therein.
However, because it exists in the subject (*dharmin*)—the living body—it is called the "uncommon inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
Furthermore, there is the uncommon [inconclusive reason], as for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is audible, like a pot and like space."
The common inconclusive [reason] is, for example: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable, like a pot and like space.
The one whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances is doubtful is, for example: "He is dark-complexioned, because he is his son."
It is like the case of his son who is currently being seen.
As was stated previously—
that the pervasion of existence with momentariness is to be apprehended through both the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*)—
what, then, is this so-called *prasaṅga*?

*Prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is the application of a consequence by means of a statement whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for the purpose of bringing about an undesirable result for the opponent;
for example, when one accepts that a universal (*sāmānya*) resides in many [individuals], the consequence of its being multiple (*anekatva*) is brought forth.
For instance: whatever exists in many locations is itself manifold, just as palm fruits contained in many vessels;
and the universal (sāmānya) exists in many locations.
Therefore, it follows by logical necessity that this [universal] must also be manifold.
Furthermore, if you do not accept that the consequence entails multiplicity,
then you should likewise not accept its subsistence in multiple locations.
Now, one might object: "If this proof called *prasaṅga* is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it lacks the three characteristics (*trairūpya*), why is it presented? [The answer is:
It is for the sake of recollecting the pervasion (*vyāpti*), just like the statement of a single part of the pervaded (*vyāpya*). As it has been said:
"Reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) [is used] because of the connection between two things; when one is absent, it serves to eliminate the other.
This is its meaning: when there is a relationship between the pervaded (vyāpya) and the pervader (vyāpaka), if the pervader is not accepted, then the pervaded must also not be accepted;
or, if the pervaded is accepted, then the pervader must also be accepted.
The established rule is that once the proponent has presented the proof (*sādhana*), the opponent must state a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) regarding it.
Refutation consists in pointing out one of the fallacies: the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), or the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). As it has been said:
"Refutations are the statement of deficiencies (*nyūnatā*) and so forth."

Regarding the refutation of the reason: if the mere pointing out of these [fallacies] constitutes a refutation, then where would fallacies such as futility (*vaiyarthya*), incapacity (*asāmarthya*), and over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) be included?
Among these three,
futility (*vaiyarthya*) is included within the unestablished (*asiddha*).
For a reason (*hetu*) is defined as that whose property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is yet to be determined.

However, where futility (*vaiyarthya*) is alleged, the definition of a reason (*hetu*)—namely, that its property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) must be doubtful—is not possible in that case; thus, it is called "unestablished" (*asiddha*). This is because the definition of the reason is unestablished. As it has been said:
"Because the statement of a reason occurs when there is doubt, a reason that is excluded [from the subject] lacks a basis."
Incapacity, however, is included within the fallacy of the unestablished nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).
For what is called the "capacity" of a reason is not something other than the very nature of the reason;
otherwise, it would follow that the reason is a non-entity.

And the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is to be included within the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it entails the possibility of the probandum-property occurring even in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), thereby transcending [the restriction to] that property.

When the negation of the self (*ātman*) is undertaken as the property to be proven (*sādhya*) with respect to a particular subject (*dharmin*), if that subject is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhitva*), the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
For example: "The self is omnipresent, because its qualities are perceived everywhere."
Therefore, in this case, even the self itself is not established for the Buddhist;
how much less will its quality of being perceived in all locations be established?
For indeed, the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas) speak as follows:

There exists a distinct substance called the *ātman*, which is separate from entities such as the body, is the agent of auspicious and inauspicious actions, the enjoyer of their fruits, and is eternal and all-pervasive.
Even if the entire universe were pervaded by it, only that living body which is appropriated by another as a locus for experience is designated as "possessing a self" (*sātmaka*).
This, however, is incorrect.
Because there is an absence of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for establishing the self;
for the self is not perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa),
since cognitions such as those of the eye are restricted to the fivefold objects of form and so forth.

Since even the mental notion of "I" has the body and so forth as its object, the notion of "I" arises in such forms as "I am fair," "I am stout," and "I am walking. As the author of the *Alaṃkāra* said:
"Even that cognition which is 'I' has the body and sense organs as its referent;
for one perceives 'I am blind,' 'I am happy,' or 'I am fair,' because [the 'I'] is experienced as having the same locus [as these]."
Furthermore, whiteness or stoutness cannot be a property of this [self] which is distinct from the body.
Nor is it logical for an all-pervading, formless entity to possess the action of moving, which conforms to material substances.
And it is not appropriate to claim that this cognition of a "lion" with respect to a young boy is merely figurative.
Because it would entail the consequence of a faltering mode of existence;
nor is it cognized through inference,
due to the absence of any logical mark (liṅga) consisting of either an effect or an essential nature.

Since no causal relationship—consisting of positive and negative concomitance—is established between [the self] and any [other entity], because the self is eternally imperceptible and devoid of distinctions of place, time, and form, the use of an effect as a logical mark (*liṅga*) is impossible.
Furthermore, since the existence of the subject (*dharmin*) itself is unestablished, a logical mark consisting of essential nature (*svabhāva*) is untenable.
Nor does any other logical mark exist.
Even by another mark, you must be pervaded by the probandum;
yet since that [probandum] is not established in any way, how can the pervasion of the mark by it be ascertained?
Furthermore, is this self of the nature of consciousness or of the nature of non-consciousness?
If it is of the nature of consciousness and eternal, then the undesirable consequence of the futility of the eyes and other sense organs is unavoidable.
If, on the other hand, it is impermanent and of the nature of consciousness, then it is merely given the name "self" of ignorance; there is no contradiction here.
But if it is of the nature of non-consciousness and is an object of perception, then its non-apprehension cannot tolerate its existence; thus, the proof of selflessness is beyond reproach.
Therefore, every conditioned thing is devoid of self.

The definition of a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) by way of the unestablished nature of its own form (svarūpāsiddhi): A reason is also a fallacious reason when it is unestablished due to the non-existence of its own form, as in: "Sound is impermanent, because it is visible."
But surely, the non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*) is also a defect, since by that too the intended object of the opponent is not established;
why then is it not mentioned?

Since this is already understood through the refutation of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason, it is not stated separately. For instance, pervasion cannot be grasped by means of two particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
because a particular characteristic, being restricted by its specific place, time, and form, lacks any continuity elsewhere.
Rather, pervasion must be grasped precisely through the universals of the probandum and the probans.

In that case, if the probans is not perceived as being pervaded by the probandum, then it would follow that something could be a probans while not being a probandum; thus, it becomes inconclusive (anaikāntika).
The determination of exclusion (apoha) and the refutation of the universal (sāmānya):
[Objection] But surely, if the universal is unestablished, [how can it be refuted]?
How, then, is pervasion—which encompasses all instances through the universals of the probandum and the probans—grasped by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
This is not a fault;
for the Buddhists do not accept that such a universal as is imagined by others is contradicted by valid cognition.
But it is not that which is established by worldly convention, characterized by the exclusion of others, and designated as *apoha*.
Now, what indeed is this so-called *apoha*? According to its conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), the external object itself, such as a jar and the like, is called *apoha*.
It is called *apoha* because that which is of a different class (*vijātīya*) is excluded from it;
or else, *apoha* is the mental image (*buddhyākāra*) according to its appearance,
because in this mental image that which is of a different class is excluded— that is, set apart.
According to reality, exclusion (*apoha*) is either a mere cessation or a negative form (*prasajyarūpa*),
based on the etymology that "exclusion" (*apoha*) is the act of excluding.
But is it not the case that, according to conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), it is indeed a positive entity?
In that case, it follows that the object is purely positive;

a positive entity qualified by exclusion (apoha) is not intended. As for the view of the proponents of the positive theory (vidhivādin), which holds that when a cow is perceived, its non-cow nature is not [perceived], and thus exclusion is determined subsequently by implication—[that is their position].

Furthermore, the view of those who maintain that exclusion by negation (*nivṛttyapoha*) is the primary meaning is that, through the power of the cognition of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the object— such as a cow— is determined as being excluded from others;
however, this is not tenable, because at the time of linguistic usage, even though [the exclusion] is present first, no such sequence of cognition is observed.

For no one, having first understood a positive injunction (*vidhi*), subsequently understands exclusion (*apoha*) through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*); nor does anyone, having first understood exclusion, subsequently understand that which is excluded from others.
Therefore, the very cognition of "cow" is said to be the cognition of that which is excluded from others.

Although it has been stated that when the word "cow" is uttered, there is no mental representation of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), nevertheless, it is not the case that the exclusion of others, which serves as a qualifier, is entirely unapprehended;
for the word "cow" is conventionally established (*saṃketita*) precisely upon a real entity that is excluded from non-cows.
Just as when the word *indīvara* is conventionally established for a blue lotus, the non-appearance of "blue" at that very moment during the cognition of the lotus is unavoidable;

likewise, from the word *go* (cow), which is conventionally established for an object excluded from non-cows, the appearance of the exclusion of non-cows (*agavāpoha*) is unavoidably simultaneous with the cognition of the cow, because the exclusion functions as its qualifier.

Just as for perception, the apprehension of absence in the form of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is nothing other than the capacity to produce a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that absence,
so too for affirmative conceptual constructions (*vidhi-vikalpa*), the apprehension of absence is designated as nothing other than the capacity for an action corresponding to them.
Otherwise, if exclusion (*parāpoha*) were not understood at the time of comprehending the meaning from the word "cow," [the word would be meaningless].
How then, by excluding others, may the cognizer apply [the term] to a cow? For if one were commanded, "Bind the cow," one might bind even a horse.
Therefore, this remains established:
The external object is established as the denotation of a word solely through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*),

and not through the vivid manifestation of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because in perception, the clearly manifest specific characteristic— which is restricted by place, time, form, and state— does not manifest [in verbal cognition].

As the Supreme Lord of Logic (Dignāga) has said: "Because an object does not appear in the cognition of one whose eyes are not engaged by the word, just as it does not appear when the object is being perceived [by the senses]."

Furthermore, if a thing were to be expressed as having its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its essence, then because it would be apprehended in its entirety, affirmation and negation would be impossible;
for if it exists, the statement "it exists" is redundant,
and the statement "it does not exist" is contradictory.
But if it were non-existent, the word "is not" would be redundant, and the word "is" would be meaningless; yet, there is indeed the employment of words such as "is" and "exists."
Therefore, it is established that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, a specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not denoted by words.

If it is argued: "Just as when the nature of a jar is apprehended by perception, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) subsequently operates upon that very same object for the sake of determining its momentariness and so forth;
likewise, once the aspect of 'treeness' has been communicated by the word 'tree,' the employment of words such as 'existent' will be for the sake of determining the aspect of existence," we say: no.
It is logical that another means of knowledge operates regarding an object whose nature has not been familiarized, because perception is non-determinative in nature (*aniścayātmaka*).
But since conceptual construction itself has the nature of determination,
once its own form has been grasped, what else remains to be grasped by another means of valid cognition?

Regarding the refutation of the universal as imagined by others: we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of such a universal as it is imagined by others— that is, a single, eternal, and perceptible entity inherent in many individuals.
Therefore, it is not tenable to establish that [universal] as being "existent" (sat).

For instance, at the time of experiencing an individual such as a cow, nothing other than the specific nature of the individual—which consists of its color, configuration, and so forth—appears in perception as a single, recurring entity.
This is because there is no such experience.

Nor is it logically tenable to postulate a universal on the grounds that it cannot otherwise be explained—that is, based on the notion that a single-form conceptualizing cognition arises immediately after the experience of individual particulars;
for this cognition arises through a causal succession from the particulars themselves, which possess powers bestowed by their own causes.
Even though they are distinct, only certain particulars are capable of producing this cognition.
Not all [causes produce the effect],
because the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva), which is observed through perception and non-perception, cannot be set aside;
and this capacity is observed to belong only to certain individuals, even though there is no difference in their distinctness (bheda).
Just as *guḍūcī*, *nimba*, and other such substances [act] in the pacification of fever and the like;

as it has been said: "Even though they are distinct, certain things are determined by their own nature to accomplish a single purpose—such as the cognition of a single object through a single reflective awareness—just like the sense organs and so forth. Thus.

Furthermore, even if a universal exists as omnipresent and distinct from heterogeneous things, when it is asked why that universal— in spite of there being no difference in its distinctness— subsists only in individual cows and produces a cognition of a single form only therein, the opponent’s answer is that it is "by its very nature" (*svabhāvena*). And that [answer] is inconsistent with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For us, however, the reply based on intrinsic nature is indeed consistent with reason, because it is not established by any means of valid cognition.
Likewise, this is another proof for establishing [the existence of] birth, presented by the opponent:
whatever is specific cognition is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of its qualifier,
just as the cognition of "one with a staff" [is preceded by the apprehension of the staff].
And this specific cognition, "This is a cow," is, in terms of its object, an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). To this it is replied:

what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is either that a specific cognition is invariably concomitant with the apprehension of distinct qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), or that it is invariably concomitant with the mere experience of the qualifiers.
In the first case, there is sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*),
because in perception, which grasps the actual entity, there is no appearance of both [the particular and the universal].
Furthermore, the reason "being a qualified cognition" would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since the universal is also a qualified cognition.
Because that [universal] is perceived even without the apprehension of distinct qualifiers,
as in the cases: "this jar possesses its own nature," or "the universal cowness."
In the second case, however, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),
because the relationship between qualifier and qualified is accepted on the basis of an imagined distinction— just as in the case of "the pot possesses its own nature" (*svarūpavān ghaṭaḥ*)—
since the conventional usage "this is a cow" is produced by the experience of the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*).
Thus, for this reason as well, the universal is not established by the aforementioned proof. Therefore, since the universal imagined by others cannot withstand analysis,

it is established that the universal— which is the mere thing excluded from what is not of that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛttavastumātra*)— is denoted by the word "exclusion" (*apoha*), and is faultlessly a factor in linguistic convention (*vyavahārāṅga*) according to its conceptual determination (*yathādhyavasāyam*).

To negate the universal (sāmānya), the formal argument (prayoga) should be stated as follows: Whatever is not perceived there, despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility, is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent" in that place;
for example, a horn on the head of a horse.

And the universal, though meeting the conditions for perceptibility, is not perceived among the individual instances (vyakti) being observed. This is a case of the non-perception of an essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi).
Nor is there a possibility of [the universal] being unestablished;
for, apart from the nature of the individual characterized by color and shape, no second recurring form is perceived in any way, even when examined with great care.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to claim that this [universal] is established by perception merely because it is not perceived, as is the case with cognition.
For knowledge is established by the means of valid cognition of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and is not graspable by visual consciousness; however,
this [universal] is graspable by visual consciousness because it is a property of the object (*artha*).
And perception is accepted by others [as a valid means of knowledge].
Thus, since the universal (sāmānya) imagined by others cannot withstand critical examination,
it is stated that the universal is merely the thing-in-itself as excluded from what is not of that nature (atadrūpaparāvṛtta).
Therefore, it is established that every conditioned entity is empty of the universals imagined by others.
The refutation of the proof for an *īśvara* (God) should also be understood as follows: it cannot be established by anyone that [the world] was created by an intelligent being.
For instance, if there were a creator of this world, he would have to be either eternal or non-eternal.
In that regard, it is first of all not logical for [the cause] to be eternal;
for if an eternal and capable agent exists, it would follow that creation, maintenance, and dissolution must necessarily occur simultaneously.

For that very nature by which he is the agent of maintenance and dissolution must also be present at the time of creation; thus, he would have to effect maintenance and dissolution at that very same time.

If it is argued that [the cause] does not act due to the absence of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), that is incorrect. For it is never deprived of a permanent auxiliary factor, since such a factor is always present;
nor is it deprived of an impermanent auxiliary factor.
Even if the auxiliary causes are impermanent, because their arising is dependent upon that [permanent cause],
it would follow that all effects, such as the instruments of cognition, would be produced simultaneously.
But surely this fault does not apply to God because He possesses intelligence;
for one devoid of intelligence would indeed produce an effect arising from His mere existence simultaneously and without succession.
However, since an intelligent being, though capable of acting, does not act because He does not will it, what grounds are there for reproaching Him?
It is said: [If you ask] why it does not produce those very desires as well, since they too are based solely upon its own existence—that is precisely the same objection against it.

Or, if you say: "Even though it possesses capacity by its very nature, this is simply its inherent character (svabhāva), namely that it does not act without an adventitious power characterized by auxiliary causes (sahakārin)," [then we reply:]
In that case, even a mother would be barren by her very nature; this too would have to be asserted by you, so this is merely trivial.

[Objection: "But surely this is the very nature of the effect: that it does not arise from the efficient cause alone, but occurs only later in dependence upon auxiliary factors; thus, there is no fault here. [Response: That is not tenable.
For if it were capable, it would produce the effect by its own power alone, disregarding dependence on auxiliary causes;
otherwise, it would follow that it lacks capability. Furthermore, it is not logical that an eternal entity acts sequentially, as sequential action is negated for what is eternal.
Because of its independence.
As Dharmakīrti, whose fame is renowned throughout the quarters of the world, has said:
"For that which is eternal, because of its independence, sequential production is not tenable."
"In both action and non-action, the two times are of a similar nature. Thus [it is said].
By this, the successive production of effects by non-momentary things such as the self (*ātman*) and by momentary things such as pots has been refuted.
Nor is there any contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) here,
because it is impossible for direct perception to apprehend a non-momentary entity.
For a momentary perception is not capable of perceiving that which is non-momentary;
for that which is non-momentary possesses an operation spanning multiple moments.
How, then, can it be grasped by a perception that exists for only a single moment?

For neither the prior nor the subsequent state appears now; otherwise, it would follow that even that [prior or subsequent state] is contemporary with the present, and it would follow that there is a perception of the limits of birth and destruction. Therefore, this direct perception is not capable of grasping any object whatsoever that pervades both prior and subsequent times.
By this refutation of the perceptual nature of recognition, its non-perceptual character is declared;
for a cognition that is immediate is indeed perception.
Furthermore, the prior state is not to be directly perceived now, but rather it is to be remembered;
and that which consists of the nature of memory is not perception.

Now, it might be thought: if this recollection does not directly perceive the present state, how can it be called "recollection" (smaraṇa), given that its very nature is the inclination toward direct perception?
As Bhaṭṭa has said:

"For memory arises regarding that which was previously cognized merely as 'that'; however, this recognition, 'this is that very same thing,' occurs when there is something in excess [of what was previously known]. Thus [it is said].
In that case, recognition would have the nature of both recollection and perception,
rather than having the nature of perception alone;
for perception is impossible with respect to an object already being recollected.
Furthermore, because recollection is impossible when [an object] is being perceived,
and because perception and recollection cannot coexist in a single [cognition] due to their mutual contradiction.

For it cannot be asserted by one who is not insane that the cognition occurs in one form while the apprehension occurs in another form; for if both recollection and apprehension were of a single object through different forms, they would be neither direct nor indirect perceptions.
Even if they were to exist, they would be both perceptible and imperceptible.
But it is not the case that what is being remembered is actually perceived, because perception is impossible [in that regard].
Therefore, the cognition of recognition is indeed erroneous.
Because it lacks an objective referent.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever is a cognition of recognition does not, in reality, have a single object, just like [the cognition of] grass and so forth that has been cut and grown again.
This cognition of recognition—the cognition that "this is that very same blue object, etc."—is the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi).

Because oneness and manifoldness are mutually exclusive, there is also a contradiction between the two cognitions that have them as their respective objects. Therefore, by the previously stated principle, the cognition of recognition [is established] through its having a single object, which is contradictory to having multiple objects.
Thus, because [the object] is pervaded [by momentariness], recognition does not subvert the inference of momentariness.

Nor is there a single objective basis even in the case of [perceiving] hair and so forth by virtue of having a universal as the objective basis, because it is the individual instances of the hair and so forth themselves that are being recognized.
If it were the universal that was being recognized, then [the cognition] would have to be "this very same hair," and so on.
"This is not that very same hair and so forth.

For this very reason, since there is a contradiction in the production of the cognition of recognition— whether sequentially or otherwise— if it were to have a single object, one should not suspect [the reason] of being contradictory or inconclusive.
Nor is recognition itself the establisher of that [identity], precisely because it is the very thing under investigation.
Therefore, this remains established: there is no eternal agent.
If an eternal creator is not the cause of the world, what then is its cause?
[This is] the establishment of the causality of the virtuous karma of sentient beings for the world.

It is the karma of sentient beings, known as wholesome and unwholesome. As it has been said: "The mind alone constructs the world of sentient beings and the world of the environment in their extreme variety;
for the entire world is said to be born of karma, and there is no karma apart from the mind."
Furthermore, relying upon the Vaibhāṣika school, the Blessed One, the Omniscient One, has said:
"Space and the two types of cessation—these three unconditioned phenomena are eternal;
all conditioned phenomena are momentary, empty of self, and devoid of an agent."
Regarding the establishment of the Omniscient One and the establishment of the succession of existences:
indeed, it is only when the Omniscient One is proven that his word is fit to be cited as an illustration.
If it is asked, "What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for proving the Omniscient One?", it is said in reply:

Whatever mental quality is produced through practice that is characterized by being respectful, uninterrupted, and long-term is capable of becoming clearly manifest, just as the form of a young woman is [to] a lustful man.
And these forms having the four noble truths as their object are mental qualities produced by the aforementioned practice; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
There is no possibility of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*) either by way of its locus (*āśraya*) or by way of its nature (*hetu*),

because the subjects— the mental aspects whose objects are the four noble truths as established through conceptual construction— and the reason, which is the mere quality of the mind, are both directly experienced within oneself (*pratyātmavedya*).
Nor is this reason contradictory (*viruddha*).
Because it is possible for [the image] to exist in the similar class (*sapakṣa*)— namely, in the form of a beloved woman—
it is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
for there is a relationship of cause and effect between the mental quality accompanied by repeated practice and the vivid manifestation, just as between a potter and a jar.

When the causal relationship is established through the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible by means of universal induction, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established because the probans—being a quality of the mind accompanied by practice—is capable of being the cause for a clear manifestation.

For instance, in the locus of pervasion—the mental image of a young woman present in one afflicted by passion—there is first the non-perception of clarity despite the quality of the mind being accompanied by attentive, uninterrupted, and long-term practice; subsequently, there is the experience of that clarity following the practice.

"Clear manifestation and cognition"—this refers to the causal relationship established by the three types of perception and non-perception, which pertains to the mental aspects accompanied by the practice of clear appearance. Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established as being comprehensive of all cases.
Therefore, because there is no lack of certainty (*anaikāntikatva*), the logical reason (*hetu*) is faultless.

Surely, by means of this proof, since one directly realizes the aspects of the four noble truths, the intended omniscient being who is established is one who directly realizes the aspects of the four noble truths,
but not one who directly realizes all phenomena without distinction; therefore, another proof must be stated for the sake of establishing that [latter].
It is said: a statement that accords with valid cognition and has a determined meaning must be preceded, either directly or through a lineage, by a cognition that directly perceives that object—
just as, for example, the statement "fire burns."

This statement, "all conditioned phenomena are momentary," is consistent with valid cognition and its meaning is certain; therefore, in terms of its referent, it is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*).
It is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because this statement possesses a true meaning by establishing the momentary destruction of all phenomena,
it is not contradictory either,
since it exists in dependence [upon those very phenomena].

Nor is there any inconclusiveness, because although mere speech may be preceded by doubt or error, we observe through perception and non-perception that speech whose meaning is ascertained and consistent with valid cognition is— either directly or indirectly— preceded by a cognition that directly perceives that object.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning [the status of] smoke and other such things as causes, which would lead to the total destruction of all causal reasons for effects.
An examination of the succession of existences:
it might be argued that the vivid appearance of an object conceived in the imagination becomes possible over a long period of time characterized by a succession of many births.
But what is the proof for the establishment of this succession of births? It is said in reply:
Whatever is a mind connects to another subsequent mind,
just like the present mind; and the mind at the time of death is indeed a mind— this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is there a deviation [in the rule] regarding the final mind of an Arhat;
for that is established by scripture alone, or because it gives rise to another mind free from afflictions,
since the cause— the presence of affliction— is absent.
The requirement for specific conditions and so forth establishes the existence of future lives.
Here, there is a common saying that all sentient beings engage in practices such as austerity, charity, and study due to the habituation of previous births.
Therefore, the proof for establishing this is stated: whatever is a mind is preceded by another mind, just like the present mind.
And since the mind exists at the moment of birth, it is, by implication, an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
An Examination of the Vaibhāṣika Position: Now, liberation arises from the direct realization of reality (*tattva*),
and reality is indeed one, as it has been said:
"Liberation is the vision of emptiness, and its purpose is the cultivation of all [meditations].
How, then, can there be the duality of the Omniscient One and the division of Buddhists?
This is not a fault, because all of this was set forth by the Blessed One in order to lead sentient beings toward the true meaning.
For instance, such is the opinion of the Vaibhāṣikas:
"Space and the two types of cessation—these three are unconditioned and eternal.
All conditioned things are momentary, empty of self, and devoid of an agent. Thus [it is said].
The view of the Sautrāntikas is that all this is merely cognition appearing in the form of blue and so forth,
and not an external object.
Because that which is insentient lacks the capacity for illumination,
as it has been said:
"Objects that produce cognitions of their own forms are visible, but they are not within the range of the sense organs."
As it has been stated by Alaṅkāra:
"If blue is cognized, how can it be called external?
If blue is not cognized, how can it be called external?"
Now, if this [object] is indeed cognition itself appearing [to consciousness],
then from where does the existence of an external object follow?
The establishment of an external object, however, would occur through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For blue and other such forms do not manifest everywhere and at all times;
nor is this tenable if they were produced solely by the power of their own material cause (*upādāna*),
because it would be impossible for them to function with respect to a restricted object.

Therefore, it can be determined that there exists for these [cognitions] something distinct from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), by whose power they arise at certain times and in certain places;
and that very thing is the external object.
Furthermore, that external object is not a composite whole (*avayavin*).
Qualities and other such properties are held by others to reside in substances,
which they claim to be of nine kinds or to consist of atoms;
however, in that regard, qualities and the rest are not [established as such].

Because they are negated precisely by the negation of substance (*dravya*). Furthermore, since inherence (*samavāya*) cannot exist in the absence of a substance that serves as its substratum, that [objection regarding] inherence is not considered here.
And substance is of nine kinds: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, direction, self, and mind.
Regarding the refutation of self, space, time, direction, and mind,
this is also a proof for the negation of the self: whatever cognition is occasional is preceded by an occasional cause,
just like the cognition of lightning.
This cognition of "I" is occasional; thus, in meaning, it is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*).
This [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because the property of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) in the subject (*dharmin*)—the "I"-cognition—is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor is the qualification "occasional" unestablished.
It is not non-existent because of the absence of the cognition "I am always [this]";
nor is it contradictory, because it is observed in similar instances (sapakṣa).
Nor is it inconclusive,
because the pervasion between occasional cognition and its occasional cause is established through perception and non-perception, just as in the case of smoke and fire;
for if an occasional cognition were produced from a non-occasional cause, it would follow that it could never fail to be produced from that occasional cause.
Furthermore, if there were uncertainty regarding the cause, it would follow that things are causeless;
likewise, if [the reason] were inconclusive, even well-established reasons such as smoke would become inconclusive,
because there would be no distinction between them.
Moreover, if the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) were preceded by a non-occasional cause, it would follow that it must arise at all times;
for a cause is defined as that which is in the state of producing its effect, and even that which does not produce it is designated as a "cause" only figuratively.

Because there is no identity between that which is acting and that which is not acting; or, if such identity were to exist, even that which is acting would necessarily fall into the state of being non-acting,
since it would possess that very nature.
Furthermore, if the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) were produced from a non-occasional cause, it would follow that it must arise all at once, because its causal complex (*sāmagrī*) would be unimpeded.
If it is argued that the self (*ātman*) is merely the objective support (*ālambana*) of the ego-sense and not its cause, we say no.
Because that which is not a cause cannot function as an object of cognition, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Now, does that which is called "space" exist as some kind of real entity,
or does it not exist at all?
It certainly does not exist.
For where there is a resistant substance, space does not grant room or opportunity;
where there is none, room is established simply by the absence of that [resistance]. So where could space grant room?
[Since space is said to be that which grants room,] therefore, if it truly existed, there would always, in every way, and everywhere be room.
But this is not the case;
therefore, we maintain that space does not exist at all.
And this refutation has been stated with reference to the Vaibhāṣika doctrine.

If it is held that space (*ākāśa*) is desired by others to have sound as its quality and that it is one, then because all sounds would occupy the same location, they could not be heard separately; consequently,
a sound perceived as being at a distance would be heard just like one situated nearby.
Nor is it the case that there is no other [cause] either; such is the certainty.
Furthermore, because space and time are unitary, the cognitions of "east," "west," "prior," and "posterior" would be untenable.
By this same reasoning, the existence of an eternal mind is also impossible.
For instance—the proponents of the mind (manas) infer its existence from the non-simultaneity of cognitions.
Indeed, many cognitions are experienced simultaneously in such cases as the viewing of a dancer.
If, however, the mind were eternal, then these simultaneous cognitions would not be possible.
Therefore, the mind also does not exist at all.
Having first refuted the composite whole (*avayavin*), the mere atoms (*paramāṇu*) are established; earth and the other elements remain,
and they are held to be of two kinds, distinguished as composite wholes and atoms.

In this regard, it has been stated that the non-perception of a well-known whole (*avayavin*), such as a jar, which is initiated by atoms through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, and which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, serves as a subverting proof (*bādhaka*).
If it is asked: "If the whole does not exist, how then does it appear as a unity?"—
Only parts appear as they are situated in such and such a way; no possessor of those parts that is itself partless is ever perceived.
Thus it has been said. Now, what indeed is this so-called "appearance of parts"?
It is simply the appearance of atoms accumulated by way of occupying various directions and locations.
If this is so, how can it be that Dharmottara stated in the *Dharmottara-ṭīkā* that "grossness is a property of the appearance"?

In this regard, the meaning is precisely this: there is no cognition of an object by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), according to the statement, "The cognition of an object would be figurative (*bhākta*).

Therefore, that which is experienced as the manifestation of blue and so forth, pervading various locations, is itself the manifestation of the gross (*sthūla*); thus, there is no fault. This applies even to those atoms (*paramāṇu*) which, for the Vaiśeṣikas, are the constituents of that [gross object].
In the view of the Vaibhāṣikas, [external objects] are within the range of direct perception;
in the opinion of the Sautrāntikas, they are inclined toward imparting their own respective forms; yet even these are not possible in the view of the Yogācāras.
Indeed, a single atom does not abide as a proven entity;
for if it were to abide in the midst of atoms situated above, below, and in the four cardinal directions, it would necessarily result in having six parts.
For that nature of its which is proximate to the eastern atom cannot logically be the same as that which is proximate to the western atom.
Because the two would have to occupy the same location.
And thus, that atom which has a nature contiguous with the preceding atom would approach the subsequent atom only if the latter were also present there.
Even in the absence of actual contiguity, this same situation applies even in the case of mere facing toward one another.
And consequently, it follows that the mass would be no larger than a single atom.
Alternatively, this is the view of the Yogācāra, or rather, this is the analysis:
that which appears here as manifold cannot logically be a single entity.
It is not manifold either, because an atom cannot exist as a plurality of atoms, as has just been explained.
For instance: if it has parts, how can it be an atom (*paramāṇu*)?

If, on the other hand, it is partless, then atoms joined together would occupy no space distinct from one another because they are joined in their entirety; thus, every aggregate would be a mere atom, such that even a mountain and the earth itself would be so.
Therefore, a distinction between those two natures must necessarily be admitted.

And just as there is a distinction between these two, so too there is a distinction between the natures of atoms situated in the directions of below, above, south, north, and so forth; thus, by the force of logic, it follows that the atom possesses six parts. As it has been said:
Through simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts;
or, because the six occupy the same location, the entire aggregate would be the size of a single atom.
Thus,
since the non-establishment of one [atom] entails the non-establishment of many as well, atoms do not exist.
If there is no external object, then what is the objective referent of this appearance?
Indeed, this appearance, proceeding from beginningless false predispositions (*vāsanā*), is observed to be entirely without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
For if there were an object, it would possess an objective basis; and by that [object], there would have to be a composite whole (*avayavin*).
Or [it may be] by an accumulation of atoms;
