yet both of these, having their forms seized by the refuting means of valid cognition just mentioned, do not surpass a lotus in the sky, as it has been said:
"There is no such thing as a composite whole, nor do atoms exist."
Appearance is without objective support, resembling the experience of a dream. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the doctrine of non-objectivity (*nirālambanavāda*),
it is well known that dream-cognition is without an external object;
moreover, there is no difference whatsoever between the experiences of dreaming and waking.
Because of the observation of similarity in every respect,
a consciousness that has not acquired a specific form due to being without an object is not capable of experiencing a connection with an object;
for that which is indistinguishable from the absence of an object is itself without an object.

Just as a second cognition arising from the sight of hair in a single patch of sky is not distinct from dream-cognition because it lacks an objective basis, so too is waking-consciousness—which is the subject of dispute—not distinct from dream-cognition due to its lack of an objective basis; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Regarding this consciousness, there is a distinction between the positions of its being with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*nirākāra*).

If external objects do not exist, what then is ultimately real? Only non-conceptual consciousness (*niṣprapañca-vijñāna*), unstained by the blemishes of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), is ultimately real. As it has been said:
"Consciousness, free from the grasped and the grasper, is ultimately real.
Furthermore, it has been said:
"There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of that [intellect] itself."
Due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper, that very [consciousness] shines forth by itself.
And this was said by the Blessed One:
"An external object does not exist in the way it is conceptualized by the ignorant;
rather, the mind, stirred by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), proceeds appearing as an object."

Regarding the view of the proponents of mental forms (*sākāravādins*), some say this: "All this that is established as the nature of all bodies and objects is nothing but consciousness; and since that is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), it is neither the grasped nor the grasper for anyone."
However, through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the state of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) is established.
Therefore, consciousness—which is devoid of the imagined state of grasped and grasper and which possesses an aspect (*sākāra*)—is the truth;
such is the view of the proponents of the aspectless (*nirākāravādin*).
Others, however, maintain that there is a real consciousness (vijñāna) which is unstained by the blemish of any mental forms (ākāra) and resembles pure crystal;
these forms, being entirely false, appear only as they are displayed by ignorance (avidyā).

Therefore, the so-called "object" (grāhya) does not exist at all; and since the object is absent, that quality of being a "subject" (grāhakatva) which belongs to consciousness in relation to it is likewise non-existent.
In the view of the Mādhyamikas, however, even that consciousness is not ultimately real, because it cannot withstand analysis;
for in the world, that which is endowed with intrinsic nature is said to be ultimately real.
Furthermore, upon investigation, no intrinsic nature whatsoever is tenable for this [entity],
whether it be one or many,
because it cannot withstand the aforementioned analysis.
As it has been said: "Even that consciousness is not accepted by the wise as being ultimately real, because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a lotus in the sky."
Kīrtipāda has also said:
"That form by which entities are conceptualized does not exist in reality,
because neither a single nor a manifold form is found among them."
Likewise, the author of the *Alaṅkāra* has also said:
"But when neither conceptual construction nor anything else possesses the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then, even though everything is falling apart, who can be blamed?"

"Even the distinction between the bound, the liberated, and so forth does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality; for indeed, no distinction appears at all to those who perceive equality everywhere. Thus it is said.
The formal argument is as follows: whatever does not possess the nature of being either one or many is not ultimately real, just like a sky-lotus;
and consciousness does not possess the nature of being either one or many—this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
First of all, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*);
for in the case of cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra-jñāna*), the incapacity for a nature that is either unitary or manifold is perfectly clear, just as it is in the case of an external object.
Indeed, that very thing which the world treats as an external object is, for the proponent of cognition with aspects (*sākāravādin*), simply cognition.
Therefore, whatever constitutes a subverting argument against its existence externally is precisely the same subverting argument against its existence internally.
For it is not accepted that what is gross can be both one and many, even if it were of the nature of atoms.
Whether this form, which consists of consciousness, is a single gross entity or many entities distinct down to the level of atoms, [it remains untenable].
In either case, the refutation pertaining to the position that external objects exist cannot be avoided;
for the refutation based on their external existence does not apply to that cognition,
such that it would occur by virtue of their [the objects'] presence.
The claim that the objection applies to that which has form, but not to the formless conscious self (*vijñānātman*), is likewise hollow;
for if consciousness possesses a form, it too must be corporeal.
For this very extension of space is what constitutes form.

The third chapter, on inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), in the *Tarkabhāṣā* composed by the Great Paṇḍita Bhikṣu Mokṣākaragupta, resident of the illustrious Mahājagaddala Monastery, is completed.
Having composed this *Tarkabhāṣā*, which consists of eight hundred and forty verses in total, whatever merit has been acquired by me,
may all the world attain Buddhahood through that merit.
Just as it was seen in the manuscript, so has it been written by me;
whether it is correct or incorrect, let no fault be attributed to me.
One should protect with great effort this scripture, which has been written with difficulty, from water, fire, thieves, and likewise from fools.
The *Tarkabhāṣā* is completed.
